title: Let them be left
hookLine: by a Highland stream a priest pleads: let them be left, the wildness and wet (Inversnaid)
tomorrow: what does faith say when no comfort is left at all?
last: IT IS MARGARET YOU MOURN FOR.

cards: Lawns get sprayed. Empty lots get paved. A patch of dandelions gets called a mess, and out comes the spray bottle again.
A priest stood by a stream in the Scottish Highlands and wrote the opposite.
At a place called Inversnaid, a brown burn comes pouring down the hill: "This darksome burn, horseback brown, / His rollrock highroad roaring down". He watches the foam spin in a black pool.
He notices the wet heather and the ferns along the banks. Then the poem stops describing, and starts pleading.

teach.b: Here's the last stanza: "What would the world be, once bereft / Of wet and of wildness? Let them be left, / O let them be left, wildness and wet; / Long live the weeds and the wilderness yet."
Why would a priest plead for weeds? Go back to the Bible's first page.

teach.h: GOD SAW THAT IT WAS GOOD.
teach.b: In Genesis, the earth brings forth grass and herbs yielding seed, "and God saw that it was good." Nobody has planted it yet. Nobody is using it.
It's good before it's useful. That's a Christian teaching about creation, and the Catholic Catechism says it plainly: each creature has its own particular goodness.
Read beside Genesis, a wild patch isn't a garden that failed. It's already doing what it was made for. Listen to the shape of the plea, too: O let them be left.

It sounds like a prayer, and it asks for nothing to be done, only for something not to be undone. That's the hard part for us. Mowing, spraying, clearing: tidying feels like caring, and sometimes it is.
The poem says sometimes the caring thing is to stand back. Not because wildness is useful to people.
The poem's own question is what the world would be, bereft of it; read with Genesis, it would have less in it of what God called good.

how: Some Christian communities keep parts of church grounds wild as care for creation, and the Catholic Church teaches that each creature has its own goodness.

games.q: what does “let them be left” mean?
o: a plea that wild, wet places be left alone
a rule for resting fields in the seventh year
a farewell to friends left behind on a trip

games.q: the burn and the weeds: tap the pairs.
p: a Highland spot where a stream pours down
a Scottish word for a stream
God's word on the grass in Genesis

s: Inversnaid ends by asking for the wild places to be tamed into gardens
it ends: long live the weeds and the wilderness yet.
in Genesis, God calls the grass and the herbs good
before any person plants them or uses them.
Hopkins valued wild places only for what they could teach people
his plea is for the wildness itself: let them be left.

games.q: a neighbor's yard has gone to wildflowers and bees, and the block wants it mowed. you're asked to sign. what fits Inversnaid's teaching?
o: wild things are good in themselves; leaving some of it can be a kind of reverence.
nature should be tamed into a neat garden to show God's order in the world.
the poem only praises Highland waterfalls; a yard isn't the wild Hopkins meant.
games.why: Hopkins asks what the world would be, bereft of wet and of wildness. Genesis calls the growing things good before anyone plants or uses them.

practice: Think of one patch near you that you've been meaning to tidy: a corner of the yard, a crack in the sidewalk with something growing in it, an overgrown pot.
For two minutes, decide to leave one bit of it wild, and picture what's living there. If you pray, you can give thanks for it just as it is.

wordCard.voice: Let them be left: Hopkins's plea at Inversnaid for the wet and wild places. Read beside Genesis, the weeds belong to what God called good.

carryVoice: Here's your line: long live the weeds, and the wilderness yet. Genesis calls the growing things good. See you soon.
